newsitem.title: CROATIA: US links new loan to handover of Croat indictee.
newsitem.headline: US links new loan to handover of Croat indictee.

text.p: The United States will probably block a pending big new international loan to Croatia if the Zagreb government does not extradite an indicted war criminal to The Hague by early May, diplomats said on Thursday.

Last month, Washington conveyed its dismay at Croatia's failure to cooperate with the U.N. war-crimes tribunal by abstaining from an International Monetary Fund vote approving a $486 million economic reform loan to the ex-Yugoslav republic.

Zlatko Aleksovski, indicted for Croat militia atrocities against Moslem civilians in Bosnia's war in 1993, was arrested in Croatia almost a year ago but authorities have not sent him to the tribunal in The Hague, claiming he is ill.

"If Aleksovski is not in The Hague by early May, the U.S. will probably end up opposing a pending new international loan of several hundred million dollars for Croatia," said a senior diplomat, who asked not to be named.

"Croatia is under serious pressure to extradite this man," he told Reuters. "Repeated promises to cooperate have not been realised, though they have given assurances Aleksovski will be extradited even this week. We hope for a breakthrough soon."
Doctors sent by the tribunal examined Aleksovski last week and pronounced him fit to travel, diplomatic sources said.
U.S. lobbying against an IMF or World Bank loan usually results in a veto since Washington is the biggest and most influential donor to both financial institutions.
Diplomats said if Washington opposed any multilateral loans to Croatia, it would have to suspend bilateral assistance too.

Washington recently approved $28 million for reconstruction of Eastern Slavonia, a former rebel minority Serb enclave of Croatia due to come back under central state authority this summer after a period as a U.N. protectorate.
The United States has granted roughly $20 million in other aid for postwar economic redevelopment in Croatia.

Bilateral assistance from elsewhere is relatively small. European Union states still keep Croatia at arm's length over its treatment of minorities, curbs on media freedom and the authoritarian rule of President Franjo Tudjman.
His nationalist government has been sharply criticised abroad for failing to make good commitments made in international peace accords to cooperate with the tribunal.
More than 70 people -- mostly Serbs with about a dozen Croats and several Moslems -- have been indicted for atrocities in the wars in Bosnia and Croatia of 1991-95.
Only seven suspects are in custody, one of them a Croat who gave himself up voluntarily.
Like the government of Serbia, Croatia has extradited no one despite repeated commitments, made as co-signatory of the Dayton peace treaty on Bosnia, to support the work of The Hague tribunal.

A U.S. law banning aid to countries that disregard the tribunal has not been enforced so far. But diplomats said U.S. patience with Croatia's failure to hand over Aleksovski and other Croat indictees was wearing thin.
"We believe the Croatian authorities have significant influence on the fate of Croat war crimes indictees (thought to be holed up in Croat-held Bosnia)," a Western diplomat said.
